history.title:
LA
BOCA
history.body:
La Boca grew where the Riachuelo bends towards the Río de la Plata, at the Vuelta de Rocha. It filled with Italian immigrants, above all from Genoa and the Ligurian coast, who worked the port, the shipyards and the boats. They built houses of timber and corrugated iron, raised on piles, out of what the shipyards and the ships left over, and painted them with whatever was to hand, mostly red and green. Many lived in conventillos: rooms on three floors round a shared patio, with one kitchen for everyone. In 1884 the neighbours founded Argentina's first volunteer fire brigade, under an Italian name and the motto "Volere è potere".

The railway cutting in this level has a real model. A branch line ran along an old stream bed there until 1928; in 1959 the painter Benito Quinquela Martín and his neighbours turned the abandoned track into an open-air museum and named it Caminito, after a tango.
history.foot: Café La Bruma and its cellar are made up.

history.title:
THE
TRANSPORTER
history.body:
The Puente Transbordador Nicolás Avellaneda began carrying people across the Riachuelo in May 1914. It was made in Britain and put together on the spot: two steel towers almost 40 metres high, standing on concrete cylinders sunk 24 metres into the riverbed, joined by a girder high above the water. A carriage ran along the girder on rails, and from it hung a platform eight metres by twelve that took people, carts, cars and even trams from La Boca over to Isla Maciel. On the first day the man driving it fell into the river, and the Prefectura fished him out.

A road bridge opened beside it in 1940, and the transporter stopped running in 1960. It is a national historic monument; in 2017, restored, it carried passengers again for the first time in 57 years.
history.foot: Its last crossing of a snowy night in 1958 is made up.

history.title:
THE
BOATMEN
history.body:
Before the transporter, and for decades after it, rowing boats carried people over the Riachuelo. The boteros took workers from La Boca to Isla Maciel and its meat-packing plants and factories, a crossing of about five minutes, at every hour of the day and night. A neighbour remembers some forty boats and ten thousand passengers a day when the trade was at its height. The boats had names, Rosa María, La Sacra Familia, Don Conrado, and they passed from father to son.

The Prefectura stopped the crossings in rain and high wind, and the boteros remember the sudestada, the south-easterly gale that pushes the river up into La Boca's streets. The boats were still crossing in 2017.
history.foot: The Santa Lucía is made up. The boats are not.

history.title:
THE
NEWSBOYS
history.body:
Boys first sold newspapers on Buenos Aires street corners in 1868, when La República paid them to, as the New York papers did, and they shouted the headlines to make a sale. They came to be called canillitas after Canillita, a 1902 play by Florencio Sánchez about a newsboy whose thin shins, his canillas, showed below his short trousers. Argentina's newspaper sellers still keep 7 November, the day Sánchez died, as their own day.

The evening papers came out in several editions a day; La Razón's evening one was the Sexta, the sixth. In 1952 La Razón put out half a million copies a day, more than any other paper in Latin America.
history.foot: La Última and its Sexta are made up.

history.title:
THE
SNOW
history.body:
Snow almost never falls on Buenos Aires: since its records began in 1906, the city's observatory has seen it settle only twice. On 22 June 1918 it began in the afternoon and came again, heavier, that night. People poured out to see it: a snowball fight in the Plaza del Congreso, snowmen, shop clerks out on the pavements, crowds in the Plaza de Mayo and the Palermo woods. Six people died of the cold, among them people sleeping in the street.

On 9 July 2007 it snowed again, for the first time in 89 years, from mid-afternoon into the night. Whole families went out into the streets and onto their balconies to watch it fall, and again people sleeping rough died of the cold. No snow fell in the 1950s: this operation borrows those two nights for La Boca in 1958.
history.foot: The snow of 1958 is made up. The snow of 1918 and 2007 is not.

history.title:
THIS
STORY
history.body:
The four neighbours, the passenger and the men hunting him are made up, and so are Café La Bruma, the Santa Lucía, La Última and the Guardia de Emergencia with its curfew. In November 1958 the national government declared a state of siege; the decree, the curfew and the Guardia in this story are invented. Porteños gave everyone a nickname, and these four are birds of the river and the city: the ovenbird, the owl, the kiskadee and the cormorant.

The rest is as true as we could make it: La Boca and the Vuelta de Rocha, the transporter and its gondola, the boats to Isla Maciel, the trams, the canillitas' cry, and the electric street lamps that men still switched on by hand, with keys, at boards on the lamp columns. The city's last kerosene street lamp had gone out in 1931.
history.foot: Lechuza is a lineman, not a lamplighter: by 1958 there were no flames left to light.

copy.title:
OPERATION
RIACHUELO
copy.briefing: La Boca, a winter night in 1958, and for the first time in forty years it is snowing. A decree keeps everyone indoors after dark, but tonight half the barrio is out in the street throwing snowballs. In the cellar of Café La Bruma, on the Vuelta de Rocha, a man is hiding from the Guardia de Emergencia, and he has to be across the Riachuelo before morning. Four neighbours take him: Hornero, who drives the tram; Lechuza, the power company's night lineman; Benteveo, who sells the evening paper; and Biguá, who rows. Put out the quay's lamps if you can, bring the passenger up, and get him over on the transporter's last crossing, or in Biguá's boat.
copy.debrief: In the morning the gondola stood at its landing and the Santa Lucía was back in her shed. At La Bruma nobody had seen anything but the snow, and the next evening's Sexta wrote about nothing else. By then the passenger was a long way off, and the snow had filled in the footprints by the river.
copy.failureNote: Lose any of the four, or the passenger, and the crossing is over. Keep to trodden slush near a patrol, keep out of the lamps and the launch's beam, and stop the clock before you act.
copy.checkpointNote: Checkpoints are also taken when the ladder is set, the cellar is opened, the passenger is up, and the gondola or the boat is ready.
